Gaussian-LIC.work: A mobile robot walks into an office building equipped only with a camera. On a typical indoor sequence where ORB-SLAM2 drift accumulates 8–12% position error over 100 meters, adding sky segmentation + exposure compensation keeps the Gaussian reconstruction visually consistent end-to-end. The result beats methods that assume ground-truth poses, showing that the rich blob representation, initialized from raw geometry, closes the loop.

The move: alternate between pose estimation via reprojection alignment and blob refinement by comparing rendered images to observations, seeding initial blobs from LiDAR points and triangulation. The operation: attach task meaning or physical state to each blob, then edit or simulate those blobs before acting. For GraspSplats, the added step is: depth-supervised blobs; samples grasps by point-tracking (no differentiable rendering); reported exact value capture; beats NeRF baselines F3RM & LERF-TOGO on part manipulation. In everyday terms, the paper changes what is stored on the blobs or how the blobs are constrained, so the scene can be tracked, edited, compressed, searched, or used for action.

Why the math helps: The robot can test an action because the scene is explicit pieces it can query, move, or compare against the live camera. The important principle is explicit representation: instead of hiding the scene inside a black box, the method keeps separate pieces that can be projected into an image and corrected when the projection is wrong.
GraspSplats.work: A depth camera (Kinect or RealSense) captures an object in 60 seconds, yielding ~1 GB of depth frames. This paper supervises Gaussians directly on depth values (not just RGB), which makes geometry crisp. Instead of differentiable rendering (expensive), grasps are sampled by point-tracking: follow a 3D trajectory through the blob cloud and check contact. On F3RM and LERF-TOGO baselines (NeRF-based methods), this approach achieves +18 percentage points higher success on part-manipulation tasks (e.g., grasping a mug's handle vs. its body). The depth supervision + point-tracking sidestep the rendering bottleneck.
GraspSplats.math: The object is a depth-supervised Gaussian set {µᵢ, Σᵢ} initialized and regularized by depth observations. The move: p(grasp|u) = 𝛑(track_points(G_render(u), I_rgb)) samples grasps by predicting point trajectories on the rendered Gaussian surface, then tracking predicted 2D points across depth frames. Why it holds: depth supervision anchors Gaussian positions and scales to metric ground truth without differentiable rendering; point-tracking grasp sampling avoids the computational overhead of inverse rendering while remaining differentiable with respect to optical flow.

Embracing Dynamics (D4DGS-SLAM).work: A standard SLAM system that tries to fit one frozen Gaussian cloud to a person walking produces a ghostly blur where the motion was—all the position uncertainty collapses onto space rather than time. D4DGS-SLAM extends Gaussians to 4D: each blob gets x, y, z, and t as independent parameters. An InfoModule then scores each blob on three criteria—how dynamic it is, whether it's visible in this frame, and how stable its optimization is—and filters out blobs that move unpredictably. On real video of dynamic scenes, the result is sharp, temporally coherent reconstruction instead of motion blur, achieving the first 4D Gaussian SLAM system.
Embracing Dynamics (D4DGS-SLAM).math: The object is a 4D Gaussian cloud G(x, y, z, t) where each blob has a time-dependent position and a learnable visibility score v(t). The move: score each blob for dynamics reliability via vi = MLP(Δxi, Δαi, Δci), filtering those with high motion magnitude or occlusion instability. Why it holds: points that move consistently across frames have stable 3D gradients; points that occlude/disocclude sharply are unreliable and removed, so only the slowly-changing cloud persists.

SharpTimeGS.work: Rendering a video frame from a frozen Gaussian cloud produces smeared ghosts wherever objects moved. SharpTimeGS gives each Gaussian blob a learnable start time t_start and end time t_end (a "lifespan")—the blob's opacity becomes zero outside that interval. When rendering frame t, only active blobs contribute. On a dynamic video sequence (say 120 frames of a person gesturing), this temporal gating replaces the smear with sharp, clean motion—blobs turn on exactly when a limb enters and off when it leaves—making temporal consistency training more tractable and final renders more photorealistic.

Why it holds: each blob only contributes where it is unoccluded and in-focus temporally; the sigmoid ramp is differentiable, so gradient descent adjusts tstart and tend to land on the true object's lifespan without smear.

Why it holds: a point moving in 3D with velocity v must project to the same object in later frames; enforcing this reprojection constraint trains 3D motion directly without external trackers.

The move: render by front-to-back alpha-compositing C = Σi ci αi ∏j<i(1−αj) and fit μ,Σ,α,c by gradient descent on photo error. Why it holds: the compositing map is differentiable in every Gaussian parameter, so the same equation that renders the scene also supplies the gradients that reconstruct it.
